preamble.summary: Chapter 22 opens with unflinching comparisons of the lazy person to filth, then moves to reflections on grief over a fool and over the dead. The central section explores the fragility of friendship -- how easily it can be shattered by betrayal or harsh words -- and concludes with a prayer asking God for a guard over the speaker's mouth and lips.
preamble.remarkable: The meditation on grief (vv. 11-12) contains a striking instruction: weep less for the dead than for the fool, because the dead have found rest while the fool's life is worse than death. The friendship section (vv. 19-26) is emotionally raw, acknowledging that some betrayals cannot be repaired and that the loss of a friend through one's own carelessness is a wound that does not heal. The closing prayer (vv. 27-30) anticipates Psalm 141:3 and is among the most personal passages in Sirach.
preamble.friction: The harsh language about fools -- compared to dung and stones -- reflects an ancient pedagogy of shame that modern readers may find excessive. The gendered language about the 'lazy daughter' (v. 4-5) is particularly pointed and culturally specific.
preamble.connections: Psalm 141:3 (set a guard over my mouth); Proverbs 27:3 (a fool's provocation is heavier than both); Ecclesiastes 7:2-4 (the house of mourning); James 3:2-10 (the untameable tongue).

verses.text_latin: In lapide luteo lapidatus est piger et omnes loquentur super aspernationem illius.
verses.rendering: The lazy person is pelted with a stone of dung, and everyone will speak of his disgrace.
translator_notes: A visceral opening image: the sluggard is not merely criticized but pelted with filth -- social contempt made physical.

key_terms.note: Literally a 'muddy stone' or dung-ball -- the lowest possible projectile, symbolizing utter contempt.

verses.text_latin: De stercore boum lapidatus est piger et omnis qui tetigerit eum excutiet manus.
verses.rendering: The lazy person is pelted with ox dung, and everyone who touches him will shake off his hands.

verses.text_latin: Confusio patris est de filio indisciplinato filia autem in deminoratione fiet.
verses.rendering: An undisciplined son is the shame of his father, and a foolish daughter will be born to his loss.

verses.text_latin: Filia prudens hereditas viro suo nam quae confundit in contumeliam fit genitoris.
verses.rendering: A prudent daughter is a treasure to her husband, but she who brings shame becomes a disgrace to her father.

verses.text_latin: Patrem et virum confundit audax et ab impiis non minorabitur ab utrisque autem inhonorabitur.
verses.rendering: A brazen woman puts both father and husband to shame; she will not be respected less than the ungodly, and by both she will be dishonored.

verses.text_latin: Musica in luctu inportuna narratio flagella et doctrina in omni tempore sapientia.
verses.rendering: Music in a time of mourning is an ill-timed tale, but the rod and instruction are wisdom at all times.
translator_notes: Timing is everything: music at a funeral is as inappropriate as a lecture at a party. But discipline is always in season.

verses.text_latin: Qui docet fatuum quasi qui conglutinat testam et quasi qui excitat dormientem de gravi somno.
verses.rendering: Whoever teaches a fool is like one who glues a potsherd together, and like one who rouses a sleeper from deep slumber.
translator_notes: Two images of futility: the broken pot cannot be reassembled, and the deep sleeper resists waking.

key_terms.note: A broken piece of pottery -- once shattered, it cannot be properly restored. Teaching a fool is attempting to repair the irreparable.

verses.text_latin: Qui narrat verbum non audienti quasi qui excitat dormientem de gravi somno.
verses.rendering: Whoever tells a story to one who does not listen is like one who rouses a sleeper from deep sleep.

verses.text_latin: Cum dormiente loquitur qui enarrat stulto sapientiam et in fine narrationis dicit quis est hic.
verses.rendering: Whoever recounts wisdom to a fool speaks to a sleeping man, and at the end of the account the fool says, 'What was that?'
translator_notes: Dark comedy: the fool listens to an entire discourse and reveals at the end that he has absorbed nothing.

verses.text_latin: Supra mortuum plora defecit enim lux eius et supra fatuum plora defecit enim sensus.
verses.rendering: Weep over the dead, for his light has failed; and weep over the fool, for his understanding has failed.
translator_notes: A parallel between death and folly: both involve the extinction of something essential -- light in one case, sense in the other.

verses.text_latin: Modicum plora supra mortuum quoniam requievit.
verses.rendering: Weep less over the dead, for he has found rest.
translator_notes: A remarkable reversal of expected grief: the dead deserve less mourning because death is rest, but the fool's living death has no such consolation.

verses.text_latin: Nequissimi enim nequissima vita super mortuum fatui quia defecit.
verses.rendering: For the worst of the worst is the life of the fool -- it is worse than death, for understanding has perished.

verses.text_latin: Luctus mortui septem dies fatui autem et impii omnes dies vitae illorum.
verses.rendering: Mourning for the dead lasts seven days, but for a fool and an ungodly person, all the days of their life.
translator_notes: Grief for the dead is bounded by the seven-day mourning period (shiva); grief for a living fool is unending.

verses.text_latin: Cum stulto ne multum loquaris et cum insensato ne abieris serva te ab illo ut non molestiam habeas et non coinquinaberis in peccato illius.
verses.rendering: Do not speak much with a fool, and do not travel with a senseless person. Guard yourself from him so that you may not have trouble, and you will not be defiled by his sin.

verses.text_latin: Deflecte ab illo et invenies requiem et non acediaberis in stultitia illius.
verses.rendering: Turn aside from him and you will find rest, and you will not be wearied by his foolishness.

key_terms.note: Related to acedia -- spiritual weariness or disgust. Prolonged exposure to folly drains not just patience but the soul.

verses.text_latin: Super plumbum quid gravabitur et quod illi aliud nomen quam fatuus.
verses.rendering: What is heavier than lead? And what is its name but 'fool'?
translator_notes: Lead, the heaviest common metal of the ancient world, becomes a metaphor for the dead weight of the fool's company.

verses.text_latin: Harenam et salem et massam ferri facilius est ferre quam hominem inprudentem et fatuum et impium.
verses.rendering: Sand and salt and a mass of iron are easier to bear than a person who is imprudent, foolish, and ungodly.

verses.text_latin: Loramentum ligneum conligatum in fundamento aedificii non dissolvetur sic et cor confirmatum in cogitatione consilii.
verses.rendering: Wooden bracing bound into the foundation of a building will not come apart; so too a heart established in thoughtful counsel.
translator_notes: A construction metaphor: the reinforced foundation resists collapse, just as a mind grounded in wise counsel resists foolish impulse.

verses.text_latin: Cogitatus sensati in omni tempore metu non depravabitur.
verses.rendering: The thought of the sensible person will not be corrupted by fear at any time.

verses.text_latin: Sicut pali in excelsis et caementa sine inpensa posita contra faciem venti non permanebunt sic et cor timidum in cogitatione stulti contra impetum timoris non resistet.
verses.rendering: As stakes on heights and unmortared stones set against the wind will not endure, so a timid heart with the thoughts of a fool will not resist the onslaught of fear.

key_terms.note: Stones laid without mortar have no binding force -- like the fool's knowledge, which lacks the adhesive of understanding.

verses.text_latin: Sicut cor trepidum in cogitatione fatui omni tempore non metuet sic et qui in praeceptis Dei permanet semper.
verses.rendering: Just as a trembling heart in the thoughts of a fool will fear at all times, so one who abides always in the commandments of God will not fear.

verses.text_latin: Pungens oculum educit lacrimas et qui pungit cor profert sensum.
verses.rendering: Whoever pricks the eye brings forth tears, and whoever pierces the heart brings forth feeling.

verses.text_latin: Mittens lapidem in volatilia deiciet illa sic et qui conviciatur amico dissolvit amicitiam.
verses.rendering: Whoever throws a stone at birds will scatter them; so whoever insults a friend destroys the friendship.
translator_notes: A simple but effective analogy: birds flee from stones, friends flee from insults. Both are instinctive reactions to aggression.

verses.text_latin: Ad amicum etsi produxeris gladium non desperes est enim regressus ad amicum.
verses.rendering: Even if you have drawn a sword against a friend, do not despair, for there is still a way back to friendship.
translator_notes: Remarkably, even violent conflict does not necessarily end a friendship -- reconciliation remains possible.

verses.text_latin: Ad amicum si aperueris os triste non timeas est enim concordatio excepto convicio et inproperio et superbia et mysterii revelatione et plaga dolosa in his omnibus effugiet amicus.
verses.rendering: If you have spoken harsh words to a friend, do not fear -- for reconciliation is possible. But if there has been insult, contempt, pride, the betrayal of a secret, or a treacherous blow -- in all these cases, a friend will flee.
translator_notes: A precise taxonomy of friendship-destroying acts: insult, contempt, arrogance, betrayal of confidence, and malicious harm. These cross a threshold from which recovery is unlikely.

key_terms.note: The disclosure of a confidence is listed alongside physical violence as a friendship-ending act -- a powerful statement about the sacred nature of trust.

verses.text_latin: Fidem posside cum amico in paupertate illius ut et in bonis illius laeteris.
verses.rendering: Keep faith with a friend in his poverty, so that in his prosperity you may also rejoice.
translator_notes: Loyalty tested by a friend's misfortune is the only loyalty that deserves to share in his later success.

verses.text_latin: In tempore tribulationis illius permane illi fidelis ut et in hereditate illius coheres sis.
verses.rendering: In the time of his distress, remain faithful to him, so that in his inheritance you may also share.

verses.text_latin: Ante ignem camini vapor et fumus ignis inaltatur sic et ante sanguinem maledicta et contumeliae et minae.
verses.rendering: Before the fire of a furnace come vapor and smoke; so before bloodshed come curses, contempt, and threats.
translator_notes: Violence is preceded by verbal aggression as reliably as fire is preceded by smoke -- a warning to take hostile speech seriously as a harbinger.

verses.text_latin: Amicum salutare non confundar a facie illius et si mala mihi evenerint per illum sustinebo.
verses.rendering: I will not be ashamed to greet a friend, and I will not hide from his face; and if evil comes to me through him, I will endure it.

verses.text_latin: Omnis qui audiet cavebit se ab eo.
verses.rendering: Everyone who hears of it will beware of him.

verses.text_latin: Quis dabit ori meo custodiam et super labia mea signaculum certum ut non cadam ab ipsis et lingua mea perdat me.
verses.rendering: Who will set a guard over my mouth, and a sure seal upon my lips, so that I may not fall because of them, and my tongue may not destroy me?
translator_notes: The chapter's closing prayer is deeply personal -- the speaker asks for divine help to control his own speech. This anticipates Psalm 141:3 and stands as the practical conclusion to three chapters on the power of words.

key_terms.note: The seal image suggests not mere restraint but authoritative closure -- only God can effectively seal the lips against harmful speech.
